item.title: 89 flights cancelled in four days, over 14,500 passengers stranded
item.description:
A total of 89 flights have been cancelled over the past four days amid continued Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, leaving more than 14,500 passengers stranded as of Wednesday afternoon.
Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB) spokesperson Kawsar Mahmud shared the information on Wednesday afternoon.
He said 39 direct flights had been cancelled, including 17 operated by Biman Bangladesh Airlines, 10 by US-Bangla Airlines, five by Saudia and seven by Riyadh Air.
Another 50 transit flights were cancelled, including 22 operated by IndiGo, four by SalamAir, one by EgyptAir, 11 by Emirates, six by Qatar Airways and six by flydubai.
Kawser said flight cancellations would continue if the situation did not return to normal.

item.title: PM meets three exemplary people for their contributions to society
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Wednesday met three inspiring individuals who have set remarkable examples in society through their dedication to education, overcoming physical challenges and planting trees.
The three are Nayla Sharaf, a BUET graduate who chose to teach at a primary school, Md Altaf Hossain, who established a school despite having no hands, and Rezaul Kibria Babul, who has planted thousands of trees on his own initiative.
They met the prime minister at his office at the Bangladesh Secretariat and became emotional at the opportunity to meet him.
Tarique listened attentively to their life struggles and initiatives for public welfare, praised their contributions and assured them of necessary support.
“People like you are greatly needed to build the country. Nation-building will become easier if everyone comes forward like you,” he said.
Nayla Sharaf completed her studies at the Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET) and joined the Local Government Engineering Department (LGED) as an assistant engineer. She later worked as an officer at Janata Bank.
Despite qualifying for the 34th Bangladesh Civil Service (BCS) examination, she chose not to join a government job and instead pursued teaching.
For the past seven years, she has been teaching at Panchananpur Government Primary School in Netrokona. She also develops teaching materials and digital content to make learning easier, particularly for disadvantaged children.
Another person who met the prime minister was Md Altaf Hossain of Narsingdi, who was born without both hands.
He learned to write with his feet and established Protiba Dukhu Mia Kindergarten School in Panchdona, Narsingdi, in 2007.
Using his savings and money from the sale of ancestral land, he built the school, which now has 145 students and 10 teachers.
He continues to write with his feet and manages various school activities despite his physical challenges.
After hearing his story, the prime minister assured him of support to construct a new school building.
Rezaul Kibria Babul of Charfasson in Bhola has also set an example through his long-standing efforts to plant trees.
Alongside his work as a mosque imam, he has spent nearly three decades planting thousands of trees along roads with his own money and labour.
After selling ancestral property to establish a nursery, he began planting saplings grown there in different areas. Many of the trees have now grown large enough to provide shade for passers-by.
The prime minister praised all three for their efforts, saying individual initiatives for the welfare of society and the country play an important role and can inspire others to undertake similar work.
He encouraged them to continue their activities and assured them of support.

item.title: 20 Bangladeshis killed in Russia-Ukraine war after 21 days of training
item.description:
Thirty Bangladeshis were allegedly trafficked to Russia on the promise of construction jobs but were instead handed over to the Russian army and sent to the Russia-Ukraine battlefield after just 21 days of military training.
At least 20 of them have reportedly been killed in drone attacks, according to a preliminary investigation by the Special Response Battalion (SRB).
The SRB’s preliminary investigation suggests the Bangladeshis were sent to the battlefield as bait to help identify enemy positions, with drone strikes enabling Russian forces to determine the attackers’ locations.
SRB-10 Battalion Commander Mohammad Asaduzzaman shared the findings at a press conference in Karwan Bazar, Dhaka, on Wednesday.
In connection with the incident, police arrested Mizanur Rahman, 55, founder of Jabal-e-Noor International, and Abu Taher, alias Lentu. The SRB identified them as key figures in the alleged human trafficking network.
According to the SRB, the 30 Bangladeshis travelled to Russia on May 7 through three organisations: Jabal-e-Noor, RS International and TS Group. Each was reportedly charged an average of Tk10 lakh on the promise of construction work.
However, after arriving in Russia, they were allegedly denied the promised jobs and handed over to the Russian army. They were sent to the battlefield after 21 days of training.
“Those who were taken from Bangladesh were not really qualified for war. They had no physical conditioning, training or tactical practice of any kind. So why were they sent after only 21 days of training?” Asaduzzaman said.
He added: “What we have understood is that they were sent to the battlefield as a kind of bait, to identify the enemy’s positions. When the enemy launches drone attacks on them, that country identifies the enemy’s location.”
The SRB said the Bangladeshis were deployed in three groups — front, middle and rear. Seventeen reportedly died in drone attacks on the first day, while three more deaths were reported later. The battalion has preliminarily confirmed the deaths of 20 of the 30 Bangladeshis.
Of the survivors, two have returned to Bangladesh with injuries, Asaduzzaman said. One of them, identified as Rajan, reportedly suffered a broken waist and paralysis of his lower body in a drone strike. He dragged himself on his chest for about four kilometres to reach a camp.
Two others are receiving treatment at a hospital in Moscow, while the remaining six are still on the battlefield, according to the SRB.
Asaduzzaman said a Russian national named Igor and a Kyrgyzstani woman named Julia were also allegedly involved in the trafficking network. Authorities are gathering information about them and conducting operations, while efforts are underway to arrest another alleged member, Mostafizur.
He added that preliminary findings suggest people from several countries have been drawn into the war through similar means.
The Bangladeshis came from various districts, including Gopalganj, Mymensingh, Narayanganj, Jamalpur, Pabna, Chapainawabganj, Faridpur, Rajbari and Gazipur.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,177 as seven die in 24 hours
item.description:
Seven more children have died from measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours leading up to 8:00am on Wednesday, raising the overall death toll from the ongoing outbreak to 1,177.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified all seven of the latest casualties as suspected.
With the latest figures, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 1,073, while the number of confirmed deaths remained unchanged at 104, as no new confirmed measles deaths were reported in the last 24 hours.
Among the seven new suspected fatalities, the highest concentration was recorded in Dhaka, with five deaths reported in both the Dhaka division and Dhaka district.
A total of 1,199 suspected measles cases were recorded in the 24 hours till Wednesday morning, taking the overall suspected case tally to 208,570.
During the same period, 128 new confirmed measles cases were reported, bringing the total number of confirmed infections to 22,840.
Since March 15, 2026, a total of 185,390 suspected measles patients have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 177,698 have recovered and been discharged from hospitals, according to the DGHS.

item.title: Fire at Drug International factory brought under control in Tongi
item.description:
The fire at Drug International's pharmaceutical factory in Tongi, Gazipur, was brought under control at 1:35pm on Wednesday after 20 Fire Service units joined a multi-agency operation to contain the blaze.
The operation involved the army, Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB), police and members of Gazipur City Corporation, alongside the Fire Service.
Fire Service Director General Brigadier General Sultanul Afrain Zunaid disclosed the information at a press briefing at the scene at 2:10pm on Wednesday.
Sultanul Afrain Zunaid said firefighting operations began on an urgent basis under the prime minister's instructions. Although the fire was brought under control at 1:35pm through the efforts of 20 Fire Service units, more time would be needed to extinguish it completely.
The fire broke out on the 4th and 2nd floors of the factory's 7-storey building. The blaze affected emergency medicines, including injections, causing breathing difficulties. No casualties were reported, but a Fire Service personnel member suffered breathing difficulties, and arrangements were made for his treatment.
He said the factory is located on Squib Road in the Tongi industrial area. The fire originated on the 4th floor of the 7-storey Unit 2 building at around 10:15am on Wednesday.
Factory workers initially tried to extinguish the fire using the factory's own firefighting arrangements. However, as the blaze intensified and the situation went out of control, the Fire Service was notified.
After receiving the information, Fire Service units from Tongi, Savar, Gazipur, Ashulia and Dhaka arrived at the scene. Army personnel, BGB members, police and members of Gazipur City Corporation also worked alongside the Fire Service to bring the blaze under control.
The incident disrupted public transport and normal life within an area of around 2km surrounding the factory.
Drug International Manager Shafiqul Islam Badal said the factory initially attempted to control the fire using its own arrangements. However, the intensity of the blaze made assistance from the Fire Service and other relevant forces necessary.

item.title: Top Indian ‘cockroach’ leaders sent to jail after protest
item.description:
Two leaders of India’s youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) were remanded in custody for five days on Wednesday, as police ratcheted up efforts to clamp down on anti-election commission protests.
CJP activists and opposition parties have defied a security crackdown to demand the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner, accusing the poll body of manipulating voter rolls to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party.
The commission, which oversees voting in the world’s most populous nation, has denied any wrongdoing.
Delhi Police said CJP leaders Ashutosh Ranka, 30, and Saurav Das, 27, were taken into custody for their “alleged repeated attempts to disturb public peace and violate the law.”
At the end of the five-day remand period, they could have their detention extended, be granted bail or be released.
On Tuesday, the pair jumped security barricades to wave the national flag at Jantar Mantar, a decades-old protest site that police have barred people from using.
“Their alleged attempts to instigate others through social media to engage in similar unlawful activities were also taken into consideration,” police added.
Parliamentary opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, from the Congress party, backed the men, who were detained after entering the site.
Jantar Mantar, in the heart of the capital, has been sealed off for days with yellow metal barricades and guarded by security personnel.
Delhi Police said on Monday it had removed the site from the list of designated protest venues.
“Waving the Tricolour at Jantar Mantar in a peaceful protest is not a crime,” Gandhi said in a post on social media. “Jailing youth for it is an act of cowardice.”
The Congress and CJP have both organized protests over the voter roll revision. Gandhi said on Wednesday that “all protests are one.”
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke praised the men, saying they “knew they could be thrown behind bars” but went ahead to wave the national flag.
“They’ve shown the entire country that the only way to stand up to a bully like Modi is to never bow down, no matter the consequences,” he said in a post on social media.
Das has worked as a journalist, while Ranka, an engineer, studied at the prestigious Indian Institute of Technology and the London School of Economics.
Rights advocates and critics say Modi’s government has eroded democratic freedoms during more than a decade in power, citing pressure on journalists, civil society groups and political opponents -- allegations the government rejects.
Human Rights Watch said Wednesday the Indian government must uphold the right of citizens to protest peacefully.
“The Modi government should stop throwing young protesters in jail and instead engage with them to address concerns over the right to vote and fairness of elections,” it said in a statement.
One of the protesters, who gave only her first name, said Wednesday she was taken to a detention center where she was beaten by police.
“They punched me here,” said Atira, pointing to her face at a news conference in Delhi, standing next to Gandhi.
“I begged them to stop, but then they started kicking me in my private parts, lower abdomen, and back. They didn’t consider me as a human.”
AFP could not immediately verify her claim.
Journalists in New Delhi marched on Tuesday to protest the detention of reporters during demonstrations. The Press Club of India said any attacks on journalists doing their jobs were “unacceptable.”
The electoral list revision, which began last year, has led to more than 133 million names being removed from voter rolls, according to media reports. Critics say the exercise has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims.
Election authorities say the move was intended to eliminate duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries.
Members of Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighboring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India’s electoral rolls.
Home Minister Amit Shah, Modi’s powerful right-hand man, dismissed the protests as localized and accused Gandhi of pursuing an “action plan to protect infiltrators.”
“The people of India are not going to fall for your deception,” he said, predicting a “resounding majority” for government in the next general election, due in 2029.

item.title: Al-Arafah Islami Bank signs agreement with United School and College
item.description:
Al-Arafah Islami Bank PLC and United School and College have signed a cash management agreement to make student fee collection easier, safer, and more technology-driven.
Under the agreement, students will be able to pay their educational fees through the bank’s branches and Islamic Wallet.
The agreement was signed by SM Abu Jafar, deputy managing director of Al-Arafah Islami Bank PLC and Abdullah Al Mamun, principal of United School and College on behalf of their respective organizations at a ceremony held at the bank’s head office on Tuesday, October 13.
The agreement will make fee payment more convenient for students and their guardians.
At the same time, United School and College will be able to access fee collection information in real time, enabling faster, more accurate, and more efficient reconciliation of accounts.
The agreement will expand technology-driven financial transactions between the bank and educational institutions.
It is also expected to contribute to the expansion of institutional cash management services and increase the mobilization of low-cost deposits for Al-Arafah Islami Bank PLC.
Among others, Md Aminul Islam Bhuiyan, deputy managing director of the bank, Mohammad Abdul Mobin, senior executive vice president, along with other senior officials from the bank and the educational institution, attended the ceremony.
The agreement is expected to further strengthen the use of digital financial services in the education sector while ensuring greater efficiency, transparency, and dynamism in fee collection and financial management for educational institutions.

item.title: Khasru: US should increase support for Bangladesh amid rising imports
item.description:
Finance Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury has said Bangladesh should receive increased support from the United States in view of improving bilateral relations and the country's growing imports from the US.
He made the remarks while briefing journalists after a meeting with officials of the US Treasury Department in Bangkok on Wednesday.
The meeting discussed debt management, US assistance and overall Bangladesh-US relations, the minister said.
He also held discussions with representatives of the US Export-Import Bank (Exim Bank) and other US agencies involved in providing assistance.
"Bangladesh did not receive much from the United States in the past. But, as Bangladesh-US relations have progressed, we are purchasing several aircraft and importing oil, soybeans and various other products and commodities from the US. Therefore, we should receive additional support from them. They agreed on this. Now, let us see," Amir Khasru said.
The finance minister said the government's economic policy prioritizes reducing dependence on loans and increasing foreign direct investment (FDI) and joint investment.
Amir Khasru said he had held extensive discussions with the US Exim Bank on the issue and hoped that Bangladesh could move forward with this approach.
"The main focus of our economic policy is investment. We want to move away from loans and focus more on direct investment and joint investment," he said.
Highlighting Bangladesh's substantial imports from the United States, the minister said purchases of aircraft, oil, soybeans and other commodities had implications for bilateral trade as well as Bangladesh's external balance of payments.
"We have strongly told them that Bangladesh is importing so much from the United States, and bilateral relations have reached their current stage. If support does not come from the US now, when will it come? The assistance we expect should come now," he said.
Amir Khasru said the relevant US parties agreed with Bangladesh's position. However, he added, the extent and modalities of the expected assistance would become clear in the coming days.

item.title: bKash, Bishwo Shahitto Kendro expand book reading program in Bagerhat and Satkhira
item.description:
In a continuous effort to foster reading habits and enlightened thinking among the students, Bishwo Shahitto Kendro in association with bKash, has expanded its nationwide book reading program in Bagerhat and Satkhira districts.
This year, 40,000 books are being distributed under this program to different educational institutions across the country.
As part of this effort, books were handed over to the students from various schools during two separate events held at Bagerhat Zila Parishad Auditorium and Shilpakala Academy, Satkhira recently.
The schools included Bagerhat Amlapara Secondary School, Bagerhat Adarsha High School, Jadunath School and College, Bagerhat Govt. Girls High School, and Bagerhat Collectorate School and College in Bagerhat district, as well as Satkhira P. N. Secondary School, Nabarun Girls High School, Satkhira Govt. Girls High School, Rasulpur Secondary School and Satkhira Collectorate School and College in Satkhira.
Golam Md Baten, deputy commissioner and district magistrate of Bagerhat; and Md Alamgir Kabir, district education officer of Satkhira attended the respective events and handed over books to the students.
Khandakar Md Asaduzzaman, executive director of Bishwo Shahitto Kendro; Sayma Ahsan, vice-president, regulatory and corporate affairs department of bKash, among others, were also present on the occasion.
To make the book-reading program more popular, a quiz competition on contemporary topics was organized for students in grades 6 to 10. At the end of the event, prizes were handed over to quiz winners.
Around 700 students attended the events.
With the aim to inculcate book reading habits and nurture human values among the students, Bishwo Shahitto Kendro has been conducting this Nationwide Enrichment program for long.
To further expand and implement this objective, country’s largest MFS provider bKash has been associated with this program since 2014.
More than 400,000 books have been distributed till now, benefiting over 3.2 million readers in nearly 3,000 educational institutions across the country.

item.title: Midland Bank launches Visa Signature Credit Card
item.description:
Midland Bank PLC has launched its Visa Signature Credit Card, providing customers with an array of premium lifestyle, travel, dining, and payment privileges.
Imtiaz U Ahmed, managing director & CEO of Midland Bank PLC, officially unveiled the new card at a ceremony held at the Lakeshore Hotel, Dhaka, on Wednesday, October 14.
Attendees at the launch included Md Zahid Hossain, deputy managing director & CRO; Md Nazmul Huda Sarkar, deputy managing director & CTO; and Md Abed-Ur-Rahman, head of cards, along with other senior officials from Midland Bank PLC.
The Midland Bank Visa Signature Credit Card is designed to deliver a premium and rewarding payment experience.
Key features include a credit limit of up to BDT 40 lakh, up to 45 days of interest-free credit, Health checkup, 8X reward points on spending, dual-currency functionality, exclusive international lounge facilities and Balaka Lounge access, convenient airport pickup & drop services, as well as attractive discounts and EMI options at various merchant outlets nationwide.
Cardholders will also benefit from an attractive welcome offer of up to 19,000 reward points, annual fee waiver facilities, complimentary buffet dining and hotel-stay privileges, travel benefits, and year-round Buy 1 Get 1/2/3 Free offers at selected leading hotels, subject to applicable terms and conditions.
Additionally, the card offers a fund transfer facility of up to 95%, insurance benefits, and convenient online shopping and payment options for tuition fees, utility bills, and mobile top-ups.
Customers can manage their card through midlandonline and enjoy NFC-enabled contactless payments.
A free Add Money facility from selected Mobile Financial Services (MFS), including bKash, Nagad, Rocket, and Upay, is also available, subject to applicable conditions.
The introduction of the Visa Signature Credit Card represents another significant achievement in Midland Bank's ongoing commitment to enhancing its card portfolio and delivering modern, convenient, and value-added banking solutions to its customers.

item.title: UCB hosts RMG Business Conclave 2026
item.description:
United Commercial Bank PLC (UCB) organized the UCB RMG Business Conclave 2026 at The Westin Dhaka on October 13, bringing together senior executives and industry representatives from the readymade garment (RMG) and textile sectors.
Held under the theme “Beyond Resilience: Building a Competitive & Sustainable RMG Industry,” the event focused on strengthening industry competitiveness and promoting sustainable growth.
Mohammad Mamdudur Rashid, chief executive officer of UCB, attended the event as chief guest.
Also present were Adnan Masud, additional managing director; Shahbaj Talat, senior executive vice president (SEVP) and head of RMG business division; and other senior officials of the bank.
A key highlight of the conclave was a panel discussion titled “The Landscape — Textile & Garments Sector: Overview, Outlook & Opportunity.”
The panel featured Riaz Shahdat, vice president of Pearl Global Group; Md Kamruzzaman Kaiser, finance director of Micro Fibre Group; Abdullah Yousuf Khan, chief business officer of Anwar Group (Textile Division); and Bishwajit Lodh, CFO of Evince Group.
The discussion focused on the current industry landscape and future opportunities, energy security, environmental, social and governance (ESG) compliance, export competitiveness, and technology-driven manufacturing.
Panelists also shared perspectives on addressing industry challenges and exploring new opportunities in global markets.
An interactive Q&A session followed, allowing participants to exchange views and experiences.
Through the conclave, UCB reaffirmed its commitment to strengthening partnerships with the RMG and textile sectors by offering tailored banking solutions, including working capital financing, trade finance and digital banking services.
The event provided a platform for industry leaders and banking professionals to exchange insights and explore opportunities to support the long-term growth and competitiveness of Bangladesh's RMG and textile sectors.

item.title: Minister: Cyber police units to expand nationwide to combat digital crime
item.description:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed has announced plans to expand the operations of the Cyber Police Unit across the country, covering central, divisional, district and upazila levels, to prevent and combat digital crime.
He said that expediting the delivery of justice requires various forms of analysis, evidence obtained through testing and proper certification. As the nature of crime evolves, plans are also underway to enhance the capabilities of law enforcement agencies to meet emerging challenges.
He made the remarks while inaugurating the newly constructed Cyber Police Center building and the digital forensic laboratory of the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) in Chittagong on Wednesday.
Ambassador of the Republic of Korea to Bangladesh Kim Ji-jun, Sayed Al Noman, MP, Inspector General of Police (IGP) Md. Ali Hossain Fakir, Additional IGP (Headquarters) Sardar Nurul Amin and Additional IGP (CID) Barrister Mohammad Mosharraf Hossain were present at the ceremony, along with senior administrative officials, including Chittagong Divisional Commissioner Dr Mohammad Ziauddin, CMP Commissioner Hasan Mohammad Shawkat Ali and District Superintendent of Police Masud Alam.
Noting that the nature of crime has changed in the modern world, the Home Minister said many crimes are now committed in cyberspace, ranging from various forms of fraud to financial crimes such as stock market manipulation.
“There is no alternative to a digital forensic laboratory for preventing and combating these crimes,” he said.
He said plans for a police cyber unit had been in place from the outset and that its operations officially began on October 1. The unit currently operates under an Additional Inspector General. The newly inaugurated digital forensic laboratory will function under the supervision of the CID. Relevant departments will continue to cooperate in digital forensic analysis and testing, as they all fall under the same ministry.
“Under the leadership of the Cyber Police Unit, we will take steps to strengthen digital analysis capabilities at every level, from the central level to the divisions, districts and upazilas,” the Home Minister said.
He added that plans were also underway to establish Cyber Police Unit laboratories at the district and divisional levels to operate as digital forensic laboratories.
He noted that the CID had been operating chemical laboratories since its inception, issuing reports on various tests, including visceral analyses. “With changing times, expanding the capacity and scope of these laboratories has become essential,” he said.
Salahuddin Ahmed said the Government of the Republic of Korea and the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA) had provided full support for the construction of the newly inaugurated building and the digital forensic laboratory in Chittagong. He thanked the Korean government, the Korean ambassador, KOICA representatives and the visiting Korean delegation for their support.
“Law enforcement agencies will be equipped with the necessary capabilities to prevent and combat crime in the modern digital world. To this end, all necessary preparations will be made, including laboratory facilities, essential equipment and other support resources, Insha'Allah,” he said.
CID sources said the department had taken steps to strengthen the police force's technical and investigative capabilities to combat cybercrime in key regions of the country, including Chittagong under the project titled “Safer Cyberspace for Digital Bangladesh.”
As online banking, mobile financial services, e-commerce and digital payment systems continue to expand, financial fraud, illicit transactions and attempts to conceal the origins of funds are also on the rise.

item.title: LPG traders call off two-day nationwide strike
item.description:
Liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) traders have called off their planned two-day nationwide strike scheduled for Thursday and Friday (October 15–16).
Selim Khan, president of the LPG Traders Cooperative Association, announced the decision on Wednesday following a high-level meeting at the Secretariat and the scheduling of a public hearing on LPG pricing for October 29.
Earlier, Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Minister Iqbal Hassan Mahmood and Commerce Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir warned of stern legal action against traders if they proceeded with the planned nationwide suspension of LPG cylinder sales and distribution.
The warning came after the LPG distributors’ platform announced on Monday a complete shutdown of LPG outlets across the country on October 15 and 16 to press home several demands.
Their demands include an end to alleged administrative harassment, a review of operators’ commission rates and the release of thousands of unused gas cylinders into the domestic supply chain.
With the strike called off, traders are expected to raise their demands and pricing concerns at the public hearing scheduled for October 29.

item.title: Dengue: Five more die, 1,920 hospitalized in 24 hours
item.description:

Among the new deaths, two were reported in Chittagong division and one each was recorded in Dhaka South City Corporation area, Rajshahi and Mymensingh divisions, it said.

item.title: Fourth session of 13th Parliament to begin Nov 9
item.description:
The fourth session of the current parliament will begin on November 9 next (Monday), according to a notification issued by the Parliament Secretariat on Wednesday.
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir has summoned the session to be held at 3:30pm on the day at the Parliament Building in the capital.
The president summoned the session in exercise of the powers conferred upon him under Article 72(1) of the Constitution of Bangladesh, said a notification signed by Md Monir Hossain, director of the Public Relations Sub-division-1 of the Bangladesh Parliament Secretariat.
This will be the fourth session of the current parliament constituted following the latest general election held on February 12, 2026.
With this, the 13th parliament is going into the session after a 60-day recess as the third session was prorogued on September 10 last after only nine sittings.
Earlier, the second session, also known as the budget session, was prorogued on July 15 after 27 working days. During that session, Parliament passed the Tk938,000-crore national budget for the 2026-27 fiscal year, the first budget under the current BNP government.
The first session of the Parliament commenced on March 12, following the general election held on February 12.
During its first session, Parliament passed 94 bills, including 91 bills against ordinances promulgated during the interim government’s tenure, and formed several parliamentary committees.

item.title: Bangladesh Women suffer 3-0 whitewash in Australia
item.description:
The Bangladesh Women's team tasted a whitewash at the hands of Australia after suffering a humiliating eight-wicket defeat in the third and final match at Allan Border Field in Brisbane.
Chasing a target of 173, Australia reached 175-2 in just 22.4 overs, with an unbeaten partnership between Annabel Sutherland and Ellyse Perry sealing the hosts' emphatic win.
Put into bat first, Bangladesh struggled early as Murshida Khatun and captain Nigar Sultana Joty fell for 1 and 3 runs respectively.
Sharmin Akter and Shorna Akter attempted to steady the innings, with Sharmin scoring 50 off 93 balls and Shorna remaining unbeaten on 54 off 71 deliveries. However, a lack of substantial contributions from the other batters saw Bangladesh dismissed for 172 in 49.5 overs.
Megan Schutt led Australia's bowling attack, taking 4-16 in her 10 overs. Annabel Sutherland and Ashleigh Gardner claimed two wickets apiece.
Australia's chase suffered early setbacks as Georgia Voll and Beth Mooney departed for 11 and 21 respectively. But Sutherland and Perry took control with an unbeaten third-wicket partnership to guide their team home.
Sutherland struck an unbeaten 74 off 52 balls, including 12 fours, while Perry contributed 65 not out from 64 deliveries, hitting eight fours.Australia had also dominated the first two matches of the series. They won the opening ODI by seven wickets after bowling Bangladesh out for 166.
In the second match, Bangladesh posted 220, thanks to Sobhana Mostary's career-best 118, but Australia chased down the target for the loss of just one wicket.

Fire safety remains a distant dream
item.description:
The 12-hour blaze that engulfed Chawkbazar markets is yet another horrific reminder of Dhaka’s woeful preparedness for fires, especially congested areas such as Old Dhaka.
Once again, firefighters battled not just flames, but choked alleys, absence of nearby water sources, and warehouses packed with volatile plastics and chemicals.
At this stage, the tragedy no longer lies in the unpredictability of the blaze, but in its utter inevitability.
For years now, investigation committees have churned out expert recommendations to secure Old Dhaka -- clear, actionable mandates. From relocating an estimated 25,000 hazardous chemical units to designated industrial estates to enforcing building safety codes to installing street-level fire hydrants to unblocking emergency exits to increasing general awareness among the citizens.
Yet, these lifesaving measures remain almost entirely ignored, gathering dust while municipal authorities default to bureaucratic inertia.
This persistent negligence is a national shame. Short-term eviction drives launched after major tragedies are routinely suspended and abandoned under pressure from business syndicates, while long-promised chemical industrial zones languish in administrative limbo.
Allowing these unlicensed, highly flammable stockpiles to exist side-by-side with sleeping families is a criminal gamble with human lives, and how we continue to normalize this defies belief.
There is no reason for the present government to allow such callous inertia. We must break this fatal cycle of post-disaster posturing and long-term inaction.
Pledges and sympathy visits to fire sites will not extinguish chemical fires. What is urgently required is an unyielding, zero-tolerance enforcement campaign, and holding those accountable for endangering lives for the sake of profit. Enough is enough.

item.title: Campus politics must give way to reason
item.description:
It is safe to say that at this point, the deepening crisis at the Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology (CUET) with regard to the new vice-chancellor (VC) has reached an alarming and unacceptable threshold.
With classes and administrative functions paralyzed as a result of prolonged student blockades, and faculty and staff declaring total non-cooperation, the situation has devolved into chaos -- one that is hurting not just education for the students of the university, but also calls to attention the politicization of our higher education institutions.
Universities are meant to be beacons of rational discourse and intellectual pursuit, not battlegrounds for toxic partisan confrontation. Unfortunately, this is something our country has consistently failed to realize, and we are disappointed that the current situation is following suit.
That the VC position in our universities has remained so politicized is nothing if not an abject failure that has hurt education in this country. Even for the present situation, entering the university flanked by political cadres and forcing entry past padlocked gates is not the conduct expected of an academic leader.
Such heavy-handed optics bear an uncomfortable resemblance to the authoritarian administrative tactics of past eras, alienating the campus community and hardening student resistance.
However, we need cooler heads to prevail and move on from this. The ongoing shutdown is adversely affecting the student body at large, disrupting academic calendars and increasing anxiety for thousands of students. Shutting the VC for hours in his office and rejecting institutional channels altogether will not resolve the underlying dispute nor bring about a productive outcome.
A solution needs to be reached, and it demands immediate, serious intervention from the government who can no longer afford to remain passive observers.
There is a chasm that needs to be bridged; CUET cannot be allowed to remain held hostage, nor can disputes and disagreements be normalized in our universities and allowed to adversely affect the future of all other students.

What is Donald Trump’s Super Intelligence Force and who leads it?
item.description:
“Bigger than the Industrial Revolution and the internet” — US President Donald Trump used a comparison borrowed from “many others” to describe artificial intelligence (AI) in his announcement of a “Super Intelligence Force.”
The president’s move to address the rapid development of the AI industry came after he met with top AI executives at the end of September — and a month before midterm elections in November. Trump has faced intensifying pressure and warnings from business and political leaders about the mostly unregulated technology.
The name echoes Trump’s September executive order renaming “Artificial Intelligence” as “Super intelligence” (SI) Jay Clayton, the director of national security and the president’s new AI czar, is the task force leader.
The task force will coordinate the government’s effort “to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence,” Trump said, and “will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans.”
Trump has made it clear he does not want regulation to “stifle” progress in the SI industry, and a reported charter for the group says it will work to prevent “overregulation and regulatory capture.”
The White House has not released any information about the Super Intelligence Force, but a copy of a charter detailing the group’s responsibilities was reported in The Wall Street Journal and Politico.
The reported document shows the task force’s scope is broad, but it names biosecurity and threats to the water supply as areas of focus. Recent cyberattacks have targeted critical infrastructure in the US.
The group is to work with some of the most important US government agencies, including the Pentagon, the Justice Department, the Department of Homeland Security and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), to develop recommendations for new laws to improve government responses.
A legal requirement for AI labs to notify the government of “breaches, hacks and jailbreaks” is to be considered, as well as the potential for automatic alerts.
“Though the labs are ultimately responsible for the risks and opportunities that their models amplify and accelerate, it is the role of the federal government to recognize and understand this era of change and to enforce our nation’s laws so that the fundamental principles of our Republic are safeguarded and advanced,” the reported document says.
The charter’s remit includes financial services, energy infrastructure, transportation, agriculture and emergency services. Trump said the task force would coordinate the government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups and religious organizations, as well as critical infrastructure providers and AI companies, though some critics noted the omission of workers.
The task force has 120 days to deliver a report on the risks of AI, focusing on potential threats to civil liberties, cybersecurity, standards for advanced models and the impacts of possible overregulation.
Clayton, whom Trump named AI czar in early October, is to chair the task force. He told The Wall Street Journal he expected AI mechanisms to be “developed in dialogue,” citing risk models the Securities and Exchange Commission, which he headed during Trump’s first presidential term, and the Federal Reserve developed for the financial industry.
The reported charter also named three task force vice chairs: Andrew Ferguson, chairman of the FTC, Emil Michael, undersecretary of defense for research and engineering, Scott Kupor, director of the Office of Personnel Management.
Ferguson is expected to oversee consumer interests and advocacy groups, according to the reported charter. His inclusion comes as the FTC investigates OpenAI, Anthropic and Metr over rogue AI agents with potentially nefarious agendas.
Michael, a former tech consultant who sat on Perplexity AI’s advisory board, is to oversee coordination with AI companies. Kupor is responsible for coordination with critical infrastructure providers and other industry stakeholders.
Key members of Trump’s Cabinet, including Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, are also on the task force. The reported charter also listed David Sacks, Trump’s former AI czar, and Condoleezza Rice, former secretary of state under President George W Bush, as external members.
The task force is to report findings and recommendations to Trump and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.
According to Politico, several key Republicans were not briefed on plans for the Super Intelligence Force before Trump’s announcement. The task force comes as leading Republican Senators prepare major AI legislation intended to mitigate the risks AI poses.
Democrats have criticized the president, with Lori Trahan, a member of the House of Representatives, telling CNN that Trump was “just talking about an AI force without any sort of durable strategy on how to do that through congressional authorization,” which felt more like a delay tactic.
“We should be passing legislation and guardrails around the frontier labs. And this doesn’t do any of that,” Trahan said.
Josh Gottheimer, another Democratic representative, told Politico he was also skeptical of Trump’s motives.
“If this is the president waking up, realizing that AI risks aren’t a hoax, and is taking concrete action to protect America, then great,” Gottheimer said. “If this is just a PR diversion and an attempt to protect his family’s investments, then I have a massive problem.”

item.title: India: Can ‘cockroaches’ threaten Modi’s political grip?
item.description:
India’s Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) may have anticipated pushback from the government after its first round of protests in July, but the scale of barricading and detentions that greeted its leaders in a fortress-like New Delhi on October 10 was unlike anything they had anticipated.
The CJP began as a satirical online movement after the chief justice of India, Surya Kant, referred to unemployed young people as “cockroaches” in an offhand remark. The name is an ironic riff on the name of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
In its latest round of agitation, they are demanding the resignation of the country’s controversy-hit Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, after more than 130 million names were reportedly removed from electoral rolls nationwide.
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, accompanied by co-conveners Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, was detained from the plane in which he landed in the national capital on Saturday.
Meanwhile, police were stationed outside the homes of several other faces associated with the movement, including social media personality Dhruv Rathee, who has nearly 20 million followers on Instagram.
In central Delhi, buses were loaded with protesters, many of whom were taken to far-flung centers, where they were kept for hours. According to local media, at least 3,000 people were detained across the city.
The protests come as Modi marks 25 uninterrupted years leading elected governments, first in Gujarat state as chief minister and then as prime minister of India.
Ironically, “this celebration has happened at the time when he’s politically at his weakest,” Delhi-based writer Nilanjan Mukhopadhyay told DW. Mukhopadhyay is the author of Modi’s 2013 biography “Narendra Modi: The Man, The Times.”
He contrasted the government’s current response with its approach in July, when thousands of young protesters took to the streets to demand the resignation of Modi’s education minister over repeated exam paper leaks.
At the time, authorities had used batons, detentions and pellets to disperse the crowds gathered in central Delhi, which had been on the streets for days.
This time, authorities shifted to mass security deployments and preemptive action on a large scale. This included notices to those associated with earlier protests, transport cuts, the internet cutoff and airport arrests.
“The government has learned from its previous experience. They didn’t allow people to sit at Jantar Mantar for any length of time, so it couldn’t balloon,” Pearl Pandya, senior analyst for Asia at global monitor Acled, told DW.
“What’s worrying is whether this becomes a playbook for the future — that you are not allowed to protest in the first place,” she added, referring to the government’s decision to remove the 18th-century observatory Jantar Mantar in central Delhi from the list of designated protest sites.
Authorities, however, have announced three new designated protest sites in the national capital.
Mukhopadhyay had a different reading of the situation. “The scale of this deployment is actually a defeat for Mr Modi,” he said.
Mukhopadhyay argued that it was already a setback for the government if it was forced to deploy security forces on such a scale in response to protests from a completely new socio-political movement.
Despite the momentum, the CJP has not been able to replicate its success from July, with the protests against Kumar being led primarily by opposition leaders and student organizations.
“Education was far more of a cross-cutting issue... the right to vote is still seen as an intrinsically political one, where it’s the opposition versus the BJP,” Pandya said.
The CJP, however, has long maintained that it is non-political. This is often cited as the reason for them amassing such a large following of young followers.
Mukhopadhyay criticized that stance, saying: “You cannot raise issues about electoral neutrality... without saying that these are political issues.”
Despite the differences between the previous round of CJP protests in July and the current wave of demonstrations, sociologist Surinder Singh Jodhka emphasized continuity.
“I don’t think they’re qualitatively different. Once again, young people are the ones who are mobilized, and they are much more encouraged because the earlier round of protests was successful,” he told DW. “And it’s also asking similar questions about institutions, about democracy, about transparency and accountability.”
“There is a new hope for those who had earlier given up on India, and felt like the right wing was in complete control,” Jodhka added.
Dismissing comparisons with volatile protests in neighboring Nepal and Bangladesh, which brought down their governments, the analysts pointed to India’s strong institutions as a safeguard against a dramatic change of government.
“India has had a very strong state system and state institutions,” Jodhka explained, highlighting that even the opposition parties were asking for “the revival of institutions, rather than an overthrow of the state.”
Pandya also stated that faith in the judiciary “would prevent these protests from tipping over into a popular revolution which unseats the government.”
Nevertheless, she said, sustained discontent “might come to bite the government in 2029... or before that in the state elections.”
It could also erode Modi’s popularity, which has been a defining feature of Indian politics over the past decade, the expert indicated.
For Mukhopadhyay, the most troubling aspect of the current protests is the erosion of the electoral body’s credibility.
Recalling the pride he felt when he registered to vote at 21, he drew comparisons with young Indian voters today. “The youngsters are now fighting for their vote.”

item.title: India festival boat capsize kills 13 children
item.description:
Rescuers dragged out 13 dead children from India’s Ganges River after an overloaded boat capsized en route to a Hindu festival, officials said Wednesday, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi expressing grief over the “deeply painful” tragedy.
The boat overturned late Tuesday in Vaishali district in eastern Bihar state, with locals rushing to pull people out of the water in the dark using mobile phones to find the bodies.
“It was dark when we suddenly heard children screaming and crying for help as the boat capsized,” Ravi Yadav, a young villager who joined the rescue effort, told AFP.
“We managed to rescue only three children, using the light from mobile phones and torches, because it was dark.”
Villager Ramlakhan Rai said the boat was “small” and “not in good condition,” saying people were crammed onto a vessel suitable for just a handful.
“It is devastating -- a few families have lost all their children,” he said.
Six people were pulled out alive, including two children reported to be in critical condition.
Medic Nirmal Kumar, from the local health center, said four children and two adults were sent to the district hospital.
“We tried our best to revive them... but 13 were already dead,” Kumar said.
Vaishali district magistrate Varsha Singh told AFP 13 bodies had been recovered.
“The loss of lives in the boat capsizing incident in Vaishali, Bihar is deeply painful,” Modi said in a statement on Wednesday, announcing compensation for their families.
“My thoughts are with the bereaved families in this difficult time.”
Boat accidents are common on Indian waterways, often blamed on overcrowding, poor enforcement of safety norms and inadequate life-saving equipment.

item.title: Police crack down on pro-Khan protest in Pakistan’s northwest
item.description:
Police opened fire at a protest in northwest Pakistan, leaving several people injured, as authorities cracked down on supporters of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan, a police official and a member of Khan’s party said.
A local member of the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party said officers “opened fire directly into the crowd” at Tuesday’s rally in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, although a police intelligence officer said they fired “warning shots” to disperse protesters.
Thousands of Khan’s supporters have marched in recent weeks in the PTI stronghold of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to demand his release, also airing anti-government grievances fueled by harsh economic conditions.
A hugely popular former cricket star, Khan has been behind bars since August 2023 and faces scores of charges ranging from corruption to treason following anti-establishment riots.
He and his legal team reject the allegations, branding them as politically motivated cases aimed at neutralizing his popularity.
A police intelligence officer in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa told AFP that more than 200 protesters demonstrated in the town of Bara on Tuesday with security forces using tear gas, batons and bullets to break up the demonstration.
“After the police used tear gas and batons, the demonstrators regrouped, apprehended police personnel and assaulted them,” said the officer, who requested anonymity.
“Other officials at the scene opened fire into the air to rescue their colleagues. The protesters also attempted to snatch weapons from the police, prompting the officials to fire further warning shots into the air to disperse the crowd.”
Eleven protesters were injured by bullets and stones, they said, adding that demonstrators vandalized an emergency services office and set fire to an administrative building.
Local PTI member Khursheed Afridi told AFP that police “opened fire directly into the crowd to disperse them, leaving more than a dozen PTI workers seriously injured.”
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa was placed under emergency rule on Sunday following days of anti-government protests demanding Khan’s release.
Local police said in a statement that they arrested 50 people in Bara suspected of terror offences, sabotage and damaging public property.
Authorities in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa have detained hundreds of PTI members since emergency rule kicked in, according to police.
Pakistan’s Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said Monday that the province’s chief minister Sohail Afridi had been placed in custody, but that he had not been “arrested.”
He did not provide further details on the detention.
The PTI’s Khursheed Afridi told AFP that more than 800 demonstrators had mobilized in Bara in support of Sohail Afridi.
Afridi is a tribal name that is common in the Khyber district in northwest Pakistan.
Islamabad has justified the imposition of emergency rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa by accusing its PTI administration of failing to deal with militant violence which has blighted the province.
The PTI has vehemently opposed the measure, describing it as undemocratic and a grab for power by the federal government.

item.title: Indonesia haze spikes Singapore pollution, shuts East Timor schools
item.description:
Air pollution in part of Singapore hit the country’s “very high” band on Wednesday while East Timor shut schools, as haze from forest fires raging in Indonesia causes a regional crisis.
The blazes in Indonesia have burned through hundreds of thousands of hectares of forest and plantations on Borneo and Sumatra islands, sickened local residents and sent thick haze across the region.
Air pollution in western Singapore on Wednesday hit “very high” -- the country’s top level -- the National Environment Agency said.
It recorded levels of tiny particulates capable of penetrating the bloodstream and lungs, known as PM2.5, at 288 micrograms per cubic meter, vastly exceeding the World Health Organization’s recommended average annual exposure of five micrograms.
Indonesia regularly battles wildfires during the dry season, but has seen stronger-than-usual blazes this year as a powerful El Nino cycle brings drought.
Experts also point to slash-and-burn land-clearing practices that have changed the naturally fire-resistant landscape of Sumatra and Borneo.
The haze has drifted into neighboring Singapore, Malaysia and East Timor, which said it would shut schools nationwide for three days from Thursday, and as far afield as the Philippines.
The closures in East Timor were necessary “as a preventive measure to protect the health of students, teachers and other members of the educational community, given current air quality conditions,” the government said.
It urged families to keep children indoors and to use “respiratory protection” if going outside.
Singapore rolled out subsidies for haze-related medical treatment from Monday, a measure last activated in 2015 when similar blazes in Indonesia cloaked Southeast Asia in toxic smoke for weeks.
The city-state has also begun distributing N95 masks to eligible residents when pollution reaches very unhealthy levels.
Singapore’s National Trades Union Congress said Monday that public transport workers and delivery riders could receive free N95 masks, but AFP found uptake was slow.
“It’s a little bit uncomfortable to wear a mask, and some orders we have to walk around blocks, or park outside,” a delivery rider, who gave his name only as Daniel, told AFP.
“With the mask, I will have to breathe heavier,” the 27-year-old said.
Ong Kwang Wei, 57, who has asthma, said he wore an N95 mask outdoors and carried his inhaler and medication with him at all times.
He was accompanying his 88-year-old mother -- also masked -- for a health check-up after a recent bout of flu.
“Once the flu kicks in my asthma is exacerbated... I get breathless, I cough, I get phlegm, so I need to use my inhaler,” Ong said.
In Indonesia, tens of thousands of people have sought treatment for respiratory illness linked to haze from fires burning in Borneo, South Sumatra and Papua regions.
On Sumatra island, a fire razed nearly 300 homes, forcing hundreds of people to evacuate, an official said Tuesday.
Residents first spotted the fire approaching their village in Bangka Belitung province on Saturday and tried to put it out themselves with portable water pumps.
But the fire continued to smoulder underground in peatland, and when the wind shifted, the flames moved towards their homes.
The local disaster agency said nearly 1,000 people fled the village.
“My house is gone,” Leni, a 55-year-old villager now staying at a shelter with her family, told AFP.
“There’s nothing left. I could only save myself and take my kids with me... I panicked and didn’t have the time to grab anything,” said Leni, who like many Indonesians has one name.
President Prabowo Subianto on Monday ordered the government to mobilize maximum efforts, with officials saying more than 60,000 personnel had been deployed to combat fires on the ground.
But efforts so far, including cloud seeding and water-bombing, have had limited success.
The haze has prompted Malaysia to request a meeting of regional body Asean, and on Tuesday Malaysian parliamentarian Syed Saddiq Rahman urged a “diplomatic protest.”
“We must send a diplomatic protest note, not just on behalf of Malaysia, but Asean. You need to treat them as an outcast in the region,” he said.

On revisiting Rabindranath's Shahjadpur
item.description:
"Five years have past; five summers, with the length Of five long winters!..."
Wordsworth's celebrated poem on revisiting Tintern Abbey is, among other things, a meditation on memory, time, and the ways in which places change and yet remain the same.
As I found myself returning to Rabindranath Tagore's Kacharibari at Shahjadpur on 25 July 2026, almost exactly a year after my first visit in July 2025, Wordsworth's subtitle came repeatedly to mind.
The distance between my two visits was not measured in years alone. It was marked by different companions, different purposes, and different modes of seeing. Yet, both visits converged in one enduring realization: Shahjadpur remains one of the landscapes through which Rabindranath became Rabindranath.
My first visit in July 2025 was a deeply intellectual and personal journey. I had the privilege of travelling with my respected teacher and mentor, Professor Fakrul Alam, one of the foremost Tagore scholars of our time.
Our conversations throughout the journey revolved around Rabindranath's years in Shahjadpur, the works he composed there, and the significance of East Bengal's riverine landscape in shaping his literary imagination.
We talked about the young zamindar-poet who arrived in Shahjadpur in the late nineteenth century to oversee family estates but left with experiences that enriched some of the finest prose, poetry, songs, and letters in Bangla literature.
Rabindranath Tagore’s sculpture at the BSCIC Bus Stop, dignified despite the disorder surrounding it. Photo credit: Shahed Akter
My second visit emerged from an entirely different context. I had been invited by the Department of Music of Rabindra University, Bangladesh, to conduct a practical examination in the morning. Once my responsibilities were completed, I devoted the afternoon to revisiting the places I had seen a year ago.
The approach to Kacharibari, however, immediately reminded me that heritage sites do not exist outside history. At the BSCIC Bus Stop, the most prominent and busiest location in Shahjadpur town, stands a sculpture of the Nobel Laureate.
The white monument rises above the crowded streets, dignified despite the disorder surrounding it. Looking at it, I recalled conversations I had earlier heard about attempts to damage Tagore-related structures after the political upheavals of August 2024.
The contrast between the streets outside and the Kacharibari compound inside was striking.
The roads leading to the complex were crowded, noisy, and congested. Motorized rickshaws, motorcycles, market stalls, and loudspeakers competed with one another in a continuous cacophony. Yet once I entered the compound, an almost monastic tranquility descended.
The previous day's heavy rain had washed the landscape clean.
The grass glowed with a fresh monsoon green. Large trees cast broad shadows across the ground. The historic two-story building stood serene and stately amidst flowering shrubs and carefully maintained lawns.
The museum itself remained closed due to reported renovation work, although I saw little evidence of active restoration. Nevertheless, the building retained an undeniable aura, as though it continued to shelter memories from another age.
Yet the most memorable discovery of the day did not involve the mansion itself. It involved water, or rather, the absence of it.
Within the compound I noticed a signboard identifying a place called Khonkerer Zola, a branch of the Karatoa, and a small, silted river. Following the path, I encountered what now appears little more than a stagnant, vegetation-covered depression. Water hyacinths and accumulated silt had almost erased the waterway from sight.
An elderly local resident told me that his grandfather had served the estate during Rabindranath's visits.
More fascinatingly, he recalled that in his own youth the channel contained clear, flowing water. He had bathed there himself. According to him, this small river was connected directly to the Karatoa, where the Tagore family's bojra , or houseboat, used to remain anchored.
Suddenly the place acquired enormous significance.
From this modest channel Rabindranath would have departed on many of his river journeys. Through these waterways he encountered the villages, peasants, fishermen, storms, sunsets, and endless horizons of rural East Bengal.
These experiences impacted his creative imagination and entered his writing in countless forms. Looking at the almost extinct river, I could not avoid a sense of loss. The elderly man lamented that the expansion of the government complex had contributed to its decline. Whether through neglect, development, or environmental change, a living historical landscape had slowly died.
My exploration then took me to another remnant of Shahjadpur's social history: the Behara Palli , the settlement associated with the palanquin bearers who once served the Tagore estate.
Rabindranath and other members of the Tagore family had allotted land to these workers, whose labour facilitated travel before modern transportation transformed rural Bengal. Today the profession has almost vanished.
Since the beginning of the new millennium, demand for palanquins in wedding ceremonies has markedly dwindled. Economic necessity has forced adaptation. Some descendants now run shops at the BSCIC Bazaar. Others commute to Sirajganj or seek employment in Dhaka and elsewhere.
There I spoke with an elderly woman. Her father-in-law, who died in the 1950s, had been one of Rabindranath's palanquin bearers.
She spoke of how older family members remembered the poet with affection and recounted stories about him to younger generations.
The conversation reminded me that history survives not only in archives and museums but also in inherited memories carried quietly across generations.
My final destination was the Karatoa River itself.
Unlike the dying channel within the complex, the Karatoa in July was vibrant and alive. From the bridge I watched the broad monsoon waters move steadily under a sky mottled with clouds and sunlight. Small boats traversed the river.
The green banks stretched into the distance. Everything seemed in motion, yet everything seemed timeless.
Standing there, I thought of Rabindranath once again. I imagined the poet embarking on another voyage aboard the family bojra , notebook in hand, observing the river that connected people, places, and possibilities.
The murmuring current seemed to carry echoes of his presence.
Without quite realizing it, I found myself humming one of my favourite Tagore songs: "Ogo Nodi Apon Bege." I cannot sing, but perhaps that was beside the point. The song arose spontaneously because the river itself seemed to be singing it.
As I left Shahjadpur, I realized that revisiting a place is never simply an act of return. The Shahjadpur I encountered in 2026 was both the same and different from the one I had seen in 2025.
It contained memories of conversations with Professor Alam, traces of historical injury and resilience, stories preserved by ordinary people, and landscapes both flourishing and fading. Most of all, it reaffirmed the profound bond between Rabindranath and the rivers of Bengal.
The poet is long gone.
Karatoa. Photo credit: Shahed Akter
The bojra no longer waits in the water. The little river that once guided it toward the Karatoa is dead. Yet Shahjadpur still possesses something precious: the capacity to make visitors pause, remember, and listen.
And if one listens carefully enough, amid the rain-washed trees and the flowing river beyond, one may still hear the distant cadence of Rabindranath's footsteps and the music of a world that helped create a poet.
Ahmed Ahsanuzzaman is professor of English and director of the Kazi Nazrul Islam and Abbasuddin Ahmed Research & Study Centre at the Independent University, Bangladesh (IUB).

RJ Mitte from ‘Breaking Bad’ to becoming a real star
item.description:
He became famous as the son in a troubled television family. But beyond the screen, RJ Mitte was telling a different story, one about courage, acceptance, and the right to be seen for who you are.
Some actors are remembered for the stories they tell. Others leave behind a story of their own. RJ Mitte was both.
For millions of viewers, he was Walter White Jr., the kind-hearted son in the hit American series Breaking Bad . But beyond the screen, Mitte was an actor who challenged ideas about disability and worked to make the entertainment industry more welcoming to people like him.
On October 12, 2026, Mitte died at the age of 34 in Brownsville, Texas. His death left fans and fellow actors mourning a life that had touched many people.
Before the world knew him as an actor, RJ Mitte was a boy born in Jackson, Mississippi, on August 21, 1992.
Adopted by Roy Frank Mitte Jr. and Dyna Mitte, he was diagnosed with cerebral palsy at the age of three. The condition can affect movement, balance, and muscle control. As a child, he wore leg braces and went through physical therapy.
His family faced other difficulties, too. When Mitte was a teenager, his mother was left paralyzed after a car accident. He took on responsibilities at a young age, helping his family and working odd jobs.
In 2006, his family moved to Los Angeles after his younger sister received an acting opportunity. Mitte began taking acting classes, mainly to make friends in his new city. He had no idea that the classes would change his life.
In 2008, Mitte landed the role of Walter White Jr. in Breaking Bad . Played by Bryan Cranston, Walter White was a school teacher who entered the world of illegal drug production after receiving a cancer diagnosis. Anna Gunn played his wife, Skyler.
Amid the family's growing troubles, Walter Jr., also known as Flynn, was a teenager trying to understand his father and protect the people he loved. His honesty and affection made him one of the show's most human characters.
The role was especially meaningful because Mitte also lived with cerebral palsy. However, his condition was less severe than his character's. To play Walter Jr., he worked to change his movements and speech to match the role.
The series ran for five seasons, from 2008 to 2013, and became one of television's most celebrated dramas. Mitte remained part of the main cast throughout its run. In 2014, he and his fellow cast members received a Screen Actors Guild Award for outstanding performance by an ensemble in a drama series.
For a young man who had started acting classes to make friends, it was a remarkable journey.
Although Breaking Bad made him famous, Mitte continued to build his career beyond the role.
He appeared in television series such as ‘ Switched at Birth’ and ‘ The Guardians of Justice’ , as well as films including ‘ The Oak Room’ and ‘ The Recall’ .
In 2026, he was promoting ‘ Talking to Strangers’ , a romantic drama in which he played Joshua, a man living with cerebral palsy.
Mitte wanted to explore different roles rather than remain known for one character. His career showed that an actor with a disability could take on varied parts and be recognized for his talent.
His death came while he was still working and looking towards new opportunities.
Mitte's work went beyond acting. He understood that people with disabilities were often judged before they had a chance to show what they could do.
He used his fame to challenge those ideas and support better representation. He served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children's. He also served as president of the Mitte Foundation, which supported community initiatives and more positive media representation of people with disabilities.
His message was simple: people with disabilities deserve respect, opportunities and the freedom to define themselves.
Through Walter Jr., viewers saw a young person whose disability was part of his life, but not his whole identity. He had feelings, fears, hopes and relationships, just like anyone else.
For viewers who rarely saw themselves represented on screen, that mattered.
Mitte helped show Hollywood why people with disabilities deserved a place in its stories, both in front of and behind the camera.
Away from acting, Mitte was building a life of his own. In October 2025, he proposed to his longtime partner, Kennedy Suarez.
In September 2026, he attended a screening of Talking to Strangers in Beverly Hills. On October 4, he also appeared at the Albuquerque International Balloon Fiesta with his Breaking Bad co-star Luis Moncada.
On October 12, news of Mitte’s death at the age of 34 shocked fans. His representatives remembered him as an actor, philanthropist, and advocate for disability rights. The cause of his death was not confirmed in the initial statements.
His death also deeply affected his Breaking Bad co-stars. Bryan Cranston and Aaron Paul shared their grief, remembering their friend and colleague. Their tributes reminded fans of the bond they had shared on and off screen.
RJ Mitte was only 34, but his impact went far beyond the screen. Best remembered as Walter White Jr. in Breaking Bad , he used his own journey with cerebral palsy to challenge stereotypes and inspire others. Though his life has ended too soon, the characters he brought to life and the barriers he helped break will remain part of his legacy. He may be gone, but the hope he gave others will live on.

item.description:
A British parliamentary delegation has discussed issues ranging from gender-based violence and land rights to visa services and international flight connectivity during its visit to Sylhet, as part of a week-long trip to Bangladesh.
The delegation from the British All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) held the engagements in Sylhet from October 9 to 11, focusing on education, employment, infrastructure, land disputes, and visa and consular services.
Before arriving in Sylhet on Friday, October 9, the delegation held high-level meetings with officials and representatives of Bangladesh’s government, Parliament and civil society in Dhaka, and with the United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR) in Cox’s Bazar.
Upon arrival, the delegation met representatives of BRAC, visited Sylhet Kidney Foundation Hospital and held roundtable discussions at the BRAC Learning Centre.
Participants in the roundtable included Sylhet Administrator Abdul Qayyum Chowdhury, Sylhet Women Chamber of Commerce President Lubana Yesmin Shampa, District Commissioner Abdullah Al Mamun and Sylhet Press Club President Moktabis Nur.
On October 10, the delegation participated in roundtable consultations organized by the Bangladesh Legal Aid and Services Trust (BLAST). Members met representatives of the Sylhet Bar Association, legal experts and tea garden workers.
Discussions focused on violence against women and girls and legal redress, labor rights and working conditions, minority group advocacy and community action.
In the afternoon, the delegation visited the Urang (Oraon) community with BRAC to learn more about issues affecting Indigenous and minority Hindu communities in the region.
The delegation also met participants in BRAC’s Ultra Poor Graduation Program to learn about development initiatives in Sylhet.
On October 11, the delegation visited BLAST’s Sylhet unit and met judicial officials, lawyers and paralegals. Discussions covered legal aid and access to advocacy and advice.
The delegation’s visit was supported by the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association UK (CPA UK).

item.title: Son kills mother, critically injures father in Kurigram
item.description:
A woman was killed and her husband critically injured after their son allegedly stabbed them at their home in Kurigram Sadar upazila early Wednesday.
The incident occurred around dawn in Belgachha Union, Officer-in-Charge of Kurigram Sadar Police Station Kamal Hossain confirmed the incident.
The deceased was identified as Munira Begum, 56. Her husband, Sardar Ali, 65, a retired textile engineer, sustained serious injuries and was taken to Rangpur Medical College Hospital for advanced treatment.
Their son, Mostakin Alam Shovon, 35, allegedly carried out the attack before fleeing the scene.
According to police and local residents, Shovon, who was reportedly addicted to drugs, had been sent to rehabilitation centres several times by his parents but repeatedly escaped. His parents were preparing to send him to a centre again, but he refused to go.
Staff from a rehabilitation centre in Sirajganj had arrived at the family's home early Wednesday to take Shovon to the facility.
Realising their intention, Shovon came out of his room and stabbed his mother in the chest with a knife. When his father intervened, Shovon stabbed him repeatedly in the abdomen before fleeing.
The rehabilitation centre staff rescued the injured couple and took them to Kurigram General Hospital, where the on-duty physician declared Munira dead. Ali was later referred to Rangpur Medical College Hospital for advanced treatment.

CCGP approves Tk1,466 C fertilizer imports from 4 countries
item.description:
The Cabinet Committee on Government Purchase (CCGP) on Wednesday approved the import of fertiliser worth around Tk1,466 crore from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Russia and Canada to meet the country’s agricultural demand.
The approval was given at a meeting chaired by Finance Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury.
The recommendations cover imports of urea, muriate of potash (MOP) and diammonium phosphate (DAP) fertilisers under government-to-government (G2G) agreements and existing contracts.
Under the proposals, 40,000 tons of bulk granular urea fertiliser containing 10% nitrogen will be imported from Saudi Arabia’s SABIC Agri-Nutrients Company for Tk220.65 crore. The price has been set at US$ 446.67 per ton.
The committee also recommended importing 42,000 tons of bulk granular urea fertiliser from Fertiglobe Distributions Limited of the UAE for Tk275.78 crore at $531.67 per ton.
Both urea consignments will be imported in the 2026-27 fiscal year.
The committee recommended importing 35,000 tons of MOP fertiliser from Russia’s JSC Foreign Economic Corporation (Prodintorg) for Tk166.10 crore at $383.80 per ton under a G2G agreement between the Russian company and the Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation (BADC).
It also recommended two separate imports of 40,000 tons each of MOP fertiliser from the Canadian Commercial Corporation (CCC) under G2G agreements with BADC. Each consignment will cost Tk188.90 crore, with the price fixed at $382.38 per ton.
The proposals allow for an additional 10% over the specified quantities.
In another proposal, the committee recommended importing 40,000 tons of diammonium phosphate fertiliser from Saudi Arabia’s MA’ADEN for Tk 425.58 crore under an agreement with BADC.
The DAP fertiliser will cost $861.50 per ton and forms the fifth lot of the 2026 supply arrangement.
The imports are intended to ensure the availability of fertilisers required by farmers for agricultural production.
